items.title: Copilot code review: Adaptive effort, secret detection, and more
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: GitHub Copilot code review now helps you catch more issues earlier, with less effort. Adaptive matches review depth to each pull request, so routine changes get a quick pass and risky changes get a deeper look. Reviews can also draw on related repositories and flag exposed secrets before they reach your main branch. Features in public preview are subject to change. Adaptive, cross-repository context, and secret detection are available to Copilot Pro, Pro+, Max, Business, and Enterprise plans. 🎯 Adaptive: The right review effort for each pull request Today, someone has to decide in settings or when requesting a review, what review effort level each pull request needs. A documentation update may only need Lite, while a change to authentication logic benefits from Max. Adaptive makes that choice for you. Copilot looks at each pull request’s complexity and risk, then reviews it with Lite, Balanced, or Max. Each review shows which effort level Adaptive picked. Adaptive is now in public preview. ⚙️ Configure Adaptive You can select Adaptive for a single pull request from the “Reviewers” bar, or set it as your default review effort in personal, repository, organization, or enterprise settings. Balanced remains the default review effort level. Adaptive never picks a level above the maximum review effort level set for your enterprise, organization, or repository. To learn more, see Configuring code review by GitHub Copilot. ⚠️ The maximum review effort level configured in Copilot code review settings determines which levels Adaptive can choose from. 🔗 Cross-repository context Changes often affect code outside the repository you’re working in. With cross-repository context, Copilot code review can read related public repositories during a review, so it can find code in other repositories that depends on your change. It can also find relevant context from documentation stored in other repositories, custom instructions and skills, and more. Cross-repository context is now in pu
items.why_it_matters: Adaptive AI code review and secret detection on PRs are relevant to gated review pipelines and to preventing leaked secrets in client repos on GitHub.

items.title: GitHub Copilot app, Microsoft Ignite releases
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: Copilot is most useful when it can work where you do. The GitHub Copilot app now supports your Azure DevOps repositories, your GitHub Enterprise Server instance, and the browser you’re already signed in to. Work with Azure DevOps repositories in the GitHub Copilot app Clone an Azure DevOps repository, ask an agent to create a branch, make code changes, and open a pull request, then see it through to completion without leaving the GitHub Copilot app. Track its status in the sidebar, click Fix on a review comment to have an agent address it, or turn on agent merge to let an agent fix CI failures and complete the pull request once your Azure DevOps checks and policies pass. Azure DevOps integration is now in public preview. To get started, open Settings > Experimental and turn on Azure DevOps integration, then go to Accounts > Add account and sign in with the Microsoft account you use for Azure DevOps. Cloud sessions aren’t available for Azure DevOps repositories. For more information, see the Azure DevOps documentation. Let Copilot work in your browser Ask Copilot to fill out forms, pull information from webpages, or test and debug the web app you’re building, right in the browser you’re already signed in to. Browser use, now in public preview, works in Chromium-based browsers, including Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge, with the GitHub Copilot extension for Chrome and runs in an isolated tab group. It also works alongside computer use. Browser use is off by default. To get started, install the extension, then open Settings > Computer Use and turn on both Enable Computer Use and Enable Browser Use. You can manage permission levels in the extension’s settings. Browser use is also available in Copilot CLI, VS Code, and JetBrains IDEs. For more information, see the browser use documentation. Bring your GitHub Enterprise Server work into the app Add your GitHub Enterprise Server (GHES) account to work with remote repositories, issues, and pull requests in the GitHub Copil
items.why_it_matters: The Copilot app adds agent-driven PR and CI-fix workflows. These are useful to compare with our agentic pipelines and matter for clients on Azure DevOps or GHES.

items.title: GitHub Copilot Evals is now in public preview
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: You can now use GitHub Copilot Evals to optimize GitHub Copilot for yourself. As your prompts, models, skills, and tools change, are you still getting the most out of Copilot? Evals helps you answer that question for the skills, agents, and MCP tools in your setup. Create an eval, inspect how they behave, and use the results to decide what to improve. What’s an eval? An eval is a repeatable test for AI behavior. You give an agent a realistic task, describe what a good result looks like, and check both the result and how the agent got there. AI output can change from one run to the next, so one good answer doesn’t tell you whether a customization works well for you. After changing a skill, agent, or MCP in your Copilot setup, rerun the same eval to check the behavior you care about and catch regressions. What you can do Ask Copilot in your own words or use the /eval command to: Create an eval for a skill, custom agent, or MCP tool in your project. Run it and see which checks passed and failed. You approve each run before it starts. Find out why a check failed and decide what to change in your Copilot setup. Compare runs from before and after a customization change to see whether it helped. GitHub Copilot Evals uses Vally, an extensible local eval tool, as its evaluation engine. Get started Install GitHub Copilot Evals where you already use Copilot: Visual Studio Code: Install the GitHub Copilot Evals extension from the Visual Studio Marketplace. Copilot CLI: Install the GitHub Copilot Evals plugin by following the installation instructions. GitHub Copilot app: Open Customize, add the github/evals marketplace, and install the GitHub Copilot Evals plugin. GitHub Copilot Evals is in public preview for Copilot Individual, Copilot Business, and Copilot Enterprise plans. To learn more, see the GitHub Copilot Evals documentation. Share feedback by opening an issue or joining the discussion in GitHub Community. The post GitHub Copilot Evals is now in public preview appeared
items.why_it_matters: Repeatable evals for agents, skills and MCP tools match our verification-over-vibes practice and are useful for clients standardized on Copilot.

items.title: GitHub Copilot Fusion updates: more availability, benchmarks, and models
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: Today, we’re expanding GitHub Copilot Fusion with new models, available on more Copilot surfaces, and results on two public Terminal-Bench leaderboards, giving you more ways to use Fusion and compare its performance. GitHub Copilot Fusion joins public Terminal-Bench 4.1 leaderboard Copilot Fusion is now listed on Terminal-Bench 4.1 public leaderboards hosted by Stanford, Harbor, and the Laude Institute: Terminal-Bench 4.1 measures how well AI agents complete hard, realistic tasks in a terminal. On Terminal-Bench 4.1, Copilot Fusion Max achieved a 71.2% resolution rate, 5.4 percentage points ahead of leading frontier models Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2, while costing 88% less than Fable 5.2 and 57% less than Opus 5.5. Independent leaderboards let you compare Copilot with other agents on the same tasks, using the same evaluation rules. Copilot Fusion is now available on web, mobile, and Visual Studio Copilot Fusion is coming to more places you use Copilot. With this release, you can select Copilot Fusion on the latest versions of github.com, Visual Studio, and GitHub Mobile beta apps for iOS and Android. Support in the production GitHub Mobile apps is coming shortly. Select Copilot Fusion in the model picker and let it choose and coordinate models for each task. You set the effort level and Copilot handles the rest. More models added With this release we are adding: Claude Sonnet 5.5 to Copilot Fusion Max GPT-6.1 Terra to Copilot Fusion High MAI-Code-2 to Copilot Fusion Standard Learn more Read more about Copilot Fusion. items.title: GitHub Copilot in JetBrains, Ignite releases
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: This update brings remote access, on-device voice dictation, and browser use controls to GitHub Copilot for JetBrains. Copilot users in JetBrains IDEs also get context usage shortcuts, historical diffs, simpler follow-up controls, and improvements to chat reliability. What’s new Cloud sandbox (public preview) Cloud sandbox runs Copilot sessions in an isolated, GitHub-hosted environment instead of on your computer. Copilot can make code changes and run commands and tests there, freeing local resources and allowing parallel sessions. We’re rolling this out in phases. Remote access (public preview) You can now opt in to remote access to make Copilot chats available in other Copilot clients, such as VS Code and the Copilot app. Discover shared sessions from remotely accessible computers, or reopen remote sessions from history to continue the conversation. We’re rolling this out in phases. Enable Browser Use in JetBrains under GitHub Copilot > Chat > Enable Browser Use. On-device voice dictation (public preview) You can now dictate chat messages on supported native plugin packages with Editor Preview enabled. Opt in and download a model to get started. Transcripts stay as editable drafts until you select Send. Split mode remote development GitHub Copilot supports JetBrains split mode remote development, with chat and editor UI running on your local client while Copilot operations run on the remote backend. Make sure you have the GitHub Copilot plugin installed both locally and on the remote backend. User experience enhancements You can manage conversations and find model options with fewer steps: Conversation timing: See timestamps on Copilot agent prompts and responses. items.title: Track Copilot code review outcomes in Repository insights
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: You can now see how Copilot code review feedback lands in each repository. A new “Repository insights” page, the first item in a repository’s Insights tab, brings Copilot code review outcomes together in one place. What’s new Repository insights show four summary signals for each repository: Comments addressed: Copilot code review comments that were acted on. High-severity comments addressed: High-severity Copilot code review comments that were acted on. Pull requests with no later human change request: Pull requests reviewed by Copilot that didn’t receive a later change request from a human reviewer. Merged pull requests without Copilot review: Merged pull requests that Copilot code review didn’t review. You can also explore: Addressed rate: The share of evaluable comments that were addressed, with its numerator, denominator, unevaluable exclusions, trend over time, and supported breakdowns. Comment categories: The types of feedback Copilot code review leaves in the repository. The same metrics are also available in the enterprise and organization repository 1-day reports (repos-1-day) in the Copilot usage metrics API. Why this matters Repository insights show whether developers act on Copilot code review feedback, whether human reviewers still request changes after Copilot reviews a pull request, and where merged work skips Copilot review entirely. Use these insights to find repositories with coverage gaps and focus enablement where it will have the most impact. Important notes You can view Copilot code review outcomes in the Repository insights page if you have read access to the repository. Enterprise owners and billing managers, organization owners, and anyone with a custom organization or enterprise role that grants the View Copilot Metrics permission can access the repository 1-day reports through the API. The Copilot usage metrics policy must be enabled to support this functionality. Visit the Repository insights documentation and Copilot usage metrics API d
items.why_it_matters: Metrics on how AI code review comments are acted on could help measure review effectiveness for clients using Copilot code review.

items.title: llm 0.37.3
items.excerpt: Release: llm 0.37.3 A bug fix release for LLM, mainly to cover a problem with the most recent Homebrew package of the software. Homebrew now ships the latest SQLite, 3.54.1, which includes a fix that broke LLM's logging code. Short version: in SQLite 3.54.0 the following SQL: select json_object('a', (select json_array(1))) Returns this: {"a":[1]} But in 3.54.1 the same query returns this: {"a":"[1]"} According to D. Richard Hipp: That was a bug fix. Per the documentation, (SELECT json_array(...)) returns SQL text, not JSON. Hence the 3.54.1 behavior is correct and 3.54.0 was a bug. The workaround looks like this: select json_object('a', json((select json_array(1)))) Tags: llm, webassembly, sqlite, generative-ai, ai, llms, d-richard-hipp
items.why_it_matters: SQLite 3.54.1 changed how json_object treats subquery JSON results, which broke LLM's logging. Similar JSON-in-SQL patterns in client code or tools could break silently after upgrades.

items.title: External sandboxes for coding agents
items.excerpt: External sandboxes for coding agents I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine. I worked on this project with Prime Radiant, the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects. My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox. To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations: external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly. external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance. external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package! Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code. The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still running: I continue to be fascinated by the challenge of safely running untrusted code. This external sandbox pattern provides a neat way to experiment with different approaches. Tags: sandboxing, security, ai, webassembly, generative-ai, llms, coding-agents, claude-code, codex, pi
items.why_it_matters: Introduces an external sandbox pattern for running agent-executed code safely and limiting prompt injection damage. It applies directly to how we run Claude Code and Codex agents.

items.title: GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol
items.excerpt: GPT‑6.2 Astra and GPT‑6.2 Sol OpenAI: We’re introducing GPT‑6.2 Astra, our new frontier model for your hardest projects, and GPT‑6.2 Sol, our efficient, versatile model for everyday work. They're available in the API as gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-sol. I shipped LLM 0.38 with support for the new models. 6.2 Astra is 80% of the price of 6 Astra - $8/MTok input and $40/MTok output, the same price as Claude Fable 5.2 (which was also 80% of its predecessor). 6 Astra and Fable 5 were both $10/$50. The cached price is an even bigger discount - $0.40/million compared to $1/million for the older model. This is great news for longer running agentic sessions. GPT-6.2 Sol is the same $2/$10 price as 6.1 Sol and 6 Sol - which are half the price of GPT-5.6 Sol ($4/$20). Here are the pelicans for GPT-6.2 Sol and for GPT-6.2 Astra. items.title: pnpm Introduces New Lockfile Format to Reduce Git Merge Conflicts
items.author: Sarah Gooding
items.excerpt: pnpm has introduced an experimental lockfile format designed to reduce Git merge conflicts by changing how dependencies are recorded.
items.why_it_matters: An experimental pnpm lockfile format that cuts merge conflicts could help teams running parallel agents and worktrees on Node projects.

items.title: Introducing eve 1.0
items.why_it_matters: Vercel has made eve 1.0 generally available. A GA product on a core platform in our stack deserves a look for possible client use, though the excerpt gives no details.

items.title: Decision-1.1 now available on AI Gateway
items.why_it_matters: Decision-1.1 has been added to Vercel AI Gateway. It is a lesser-known model with unclear relevance to coding or client work.

items.title: GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol now available on AI Gateway
items.why_it_matters: GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol are now on Vercel AI Gateway. These are new OpenAI frontier models available through a platform we already use, relevant for coding and client LLM features.

items.title: MAI-Image-2.7 and MAI-Image-2.7-Flash now available on AI Gateway
items.why_it_matters: Microsoft image models added to Vercel AI Gateway. This is of marginal use beyond image-generation features in client products.

items.title: Native lint and typecheck Deployment Checks are being deprecated
items.author: Cody Wong
items.why_it_matters: Vercel is deprecating native lint and typecheck Deployment Checks. Client projects relying on them need those checks moved into GitHub Actions or another CI step.

items.title: Pull-request-only preset now available for preview builds
items.author: Mehul Kar
items.why_it_matters: A new Vercel preset limits preview builds to pull requests. That can cut build minutes and noise on the client projects we deploy to Vercel.

items.title: Single-second static deployments now support more assets
items.author: Melkey Moksyakov
items.why_it_matters: Small Vercel platform improvement: fast static deployments now cover more asset types. Useful to know for client sites hosted on Vercel, but minor.

items.title: Standard builds move to usage-based billing for new teams
items.why_it_matters: New Vercel teams now pay for standard builds by usage. This affects cost estimates when we set up client projects on Vercel.

items.title: Vercel Blob now supports TTLs for automatic deletion
items.author: Agustin Falco
items.why_it_matters: Vercel Blob TTLs allow automatic deletion of temporary files, a practical feature for our Vercel-hosted client apps and data retention needs.

items.title: Vercel Sandbox Python SDK 1.0 is now available
items.author: Scott Trinh
items.why_it_matters: Vercel Sandbox now has a stable 1.0 Python SDK for running untrusted or agent-generated code in isolation. Relevant to our Vercel stack and to building AI features in Python.

items.title: Highly classified US national security communications network goes down
items.author: monkeydust
items.excerpt: https://www.reuters.com/technology/highly-classified-us-nati... Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50532849 Points: 384 # Comments: 496
items.why_it_matters: Government network outage news with no bearing on our stack or software delivery.

items.title: New StepSecurity Control: Audit GitHub Fork PR Workflow Approval Policies
items.excerpt: StepSecurity’s new control flags GitHub organizations and public repositories that let fork pull request workflows run without approval.
items.why_it_matters: Fork PR workflows that run without approval are a real GitHub Actions supply-chain risk. A useful prompt to audit our own and client org settings.

items.title: OPTIMJACK: Optimizely-Hosted Scripts Loaded a Crypto Clipper and Card Skimmer on 178 Organizations
items.excerpt: Optimizely confirmed an attacker injected malicious JavaScript into customer projects. What the payload does, who was hit, and what to check.
items.why_it_matters: A supply-chain attack injected skimmer and clipper JavaScript through Optimizely-hosted scripts on 178 organizations. Clients using third-party scripts should audit them and review their CSP.

items.title: WPPConnect Compromised: Malicious Releases Steal Secrets and WhatsApp Sessions Through the Project's Own Pipeline
items.excerpt: Malicious WPPConnect npm releases 2.4.1 and 2.10.82 steal secrets and WhatsApp sessions via Telegram. Affected versions, how they shipped and what to rotate.
items.why_it_matters: npm supply-chain compromise via the project's own release pipeline, stealing secrets. Check client projects for WPPConnect 2.4.1 or 2.10.82 and rotate credentials if affected.

items.title: A season on the farm with AI
items.author: Claude
items.excerpt: Martina Wanis is a biologist from Vienna who grows sweet potatoes in Slovenia. This year, she took Claude along for the whole season.
items.why_it_matters: Consumer marketing video about a farmer using Claude, with no engineering relevance.
